planting.note: Set out transplants after the last frost into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; give this selection a bit more room than trailing rose vervains since its habit is fuller and more upright.

directions: Site in full sun with excellent drainage, since this North Carolina selection of the native rose vervain flowers most heavily and resists crown rot best in lean, well-aerated ground. Its habit is denser and more upright than typical trailing rose vervain cultivars, and pure white flower clusters appear from very early spring and continue in flushes into fall, slowing only during peak summer heat. Established plants tolerate considerable drought and neglect, and a light shearing after the first big spring flush helps renew bloom for summer and fall. Deer and rabbits generally leave it alone, while bees and butterflies visit it readily even though the flowers are white.

common_name: Homestead Hot Pink Verbena (Patented Vivid Pink Groundcover Verbena)

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts after the last frost in average, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants to allow the low, spreading mat to knit together within a season.

directions: This US-patented sibling of the classic 'Homestead Purple' was bred for the same tough, spreading habit but with saturated hot-pink flower clusters instead of purple, and it carries improved resistance to powdery mildew from its breeding program parentage. Grow it in lean to average soil with sharp drainage in full sun, where it forms a dense, low mat that hugs the ground and covers itself in bloom from spring through frost. It is notably heat- and drought-tolerant once rooted in, shrugs off deer and rabbit browsing, and draws hummingbirds and butterflies to its abundant flower heads. An occasional trim after the heaviest flushes keeps the mat tight and encourages continued flowering.

common_name: Summer Blaze Verbena (Cherry-Red Groundcover Rose Vervain)

planting.note: Plant after the last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; give it room to trail and spread, since it fills in faster and wider than compact rose vervain selections.

directions: Also sold as 'Clear Red', this vigorous rose vervain selection produces dense clusters of bright cherry-red flowers over semi-evergreen foliage from late spring through frost. It performs best in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun, where its trailing stems root as they spread to form a broad, weed-suppressing groundcover. It handles heat and drought with ease once established and rebounds quickly from a hard shearing if it becomes leggy in midsummer. In milder climates the foliage persists through winter, giving the planting a head start the following spring.

common_name: Superbena Sparkling Rosé Verbena (Bicolor Soft Pink-and-White Spreading Verbena)

planting.note: Set out after the last frost in full sun with sharp drainage; the mounding-trailing habit makes this a strong spiller for mixed containers as well as a landscape groundcover.

directions: This bicolor Superbena series introduction covers itself in soft blush-pink flower clusters brushed with white, giving a shimmering, two-toned effect distinct from the solid-color Superbena Royale line. It is self-cleaning and needs no deadheading to keep producing new flower heads through the heat of summer. Grow in well-drained soil in full sun and let the surface dry between waterings, since it tolerates dry, lean conditions far better than soggy ones. Its mildew tolerance and heat resistance make it dependable in humid climates where older seed-grown verbenas often decline by midsummer.

common_name: Superbena Royale Chambray Verbena (Periwinkle-Blue Compact Spreading Verbena)

planting.note: Plant after the last frost in full sun in moderately fertile, well-drained soil; its more compact habit suits smaller containers and front-of-border spots as well as open beds.

directions: Chambray stands out in the Superbena Royale line for its silvery periwinkle-blue flower clusters, a cool tone that combines well with deep burgundy, chartreuse, or white companions in mixed plantings. Its habit runs a touch more compact than other Royale colors, which suits it to hanging baskets and smaller combination pots as well as landscape edging. Grow in full sun with amply drained soil, allow the surface to dry between waterings, and expect strong resistance to powdery mildew and continuous self-cleaning bloom through summer heat. No deadheading is required, and light pinching after a flush of flowers keeps the plant dense.

common_name: Superbena Royale Peachy Keen Verbena (Peach-Orange Large-Flowered Spreading Verbena)

planting.note: Plant after the last frost in full sun with excellent drainage; the warm peach-orange flower color pairs well with blue, purple, or chartreuse companions in beds and containers.

directions: Peachy Keen brings a rare warm peach-orange tone to the large-flowered Superbena Royale line, standing out against the more common purples, reds, and pinks of most verbena cultivars. Grow it in full sun in well-drained soil, watering deeply but infrequently to avoid the crown and root rot that plague verbena in soggy conditions. Like other Royale selections it is self-cleaning and heat tolerant, holding its color and vigor through the hottest weeks of summer without deadheading. Good air movement between plants helps it resist the powdery mildew that shortens the season for many older verbena varieties.

common_name: Superbena Royale Plum Wine Verbena (Deep Wine-Purple Large-Flowered Spreading Verbena)

planting.note: Plant after the last frost in full sun in well-drained soil; its rich, deep flower color reads especially well in fall container plantings and against light-colored foliage companions.

directions: Plum Wine carries deep wine-purple flower clusters that darken further as temperatures cool, making it a favorite for extending color into fall container displays and landscape beds. It shares the Superbena Royale line's vigorous, mounding-trailing habit and covers itself in bloom from planting until frost without deadheading. Grow in full sun with sharply drained soil, since wet feet quickly invite crown rot and mildew in this genus. Once established, it tolerates heat and short dry spells well, though regular watering during extended drought keeps flowering dense.

common_name: Lanai Royal Purple with Eye Verbena (Deep Purple White-Eyed Trailing Verbena)
scientific_name: Verbena hybrida 'Lanai Royal Purple with Eye'

planting.note: Plant after the last frost in full sun with sharp drainage; its cascading habit makes it a strong choice for hanging baskets and window boxes as well as landscape edging.

directions: This Lanai series selection produces deep royal-purple flower clusters, each marked with a small white eye that gives the flower heads extra depth and contrast from a distance. Its trailing stems cascade cleanly over the edges of hanging baskets and window boxes, and the strong disease resistance bred into the Lanai line keeps foliage clean through humid summers. Grow in full sun in well-drained potting mix or garden soil, watering when the top inch dries rather than on a fixed schedule. Trim back lightly if stems become sparse at the base to encourage fresh branching and continued bloom.

common_name: EnduraScape Blue Verbena (Violet-Blue Mildew-Resistant Landscape Verbena)

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts after the last frost in well-drained, average soil in full sun; its bright violet-blue flowers give strong color contrast against warm-toned companions in mass plantings.

directions: Blue is one of the original color releases in the EnduraScape line, bred specifically to resist the powdery mildew that shortens the bloom season of older verbena cultivars in humid climates. It forms a dense, ground-hugging carpet of bright violet-blue flowers that holds up through summer heat with minimal maintenance. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and water deeply but infrequently once roots are established, since it tolerates dry spells far better than wet, poorly drained ground. A light shearing after the first big spring flush keeps the mat tight and promotes continued heavy bloom into fall.
